## Remarks

The first diagram displays the open deformation family $D_i=M\setminus B$,
with structure map $p$ induced by $M\to\mathbb P^1$. Both squares are
Cartesian: $j$ includes the special fibre, while $u$ includes the complement
of that fibre. Here $\mathbb A^1=\mathbb P^1\setminus\{\infty\}$; the local
parameter $t$ used above vanishes at $\infty$, not at the origin of this
ordinary-fibre chart.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large, labels={font=\large}]
C_XY \arrow[r, hook, "j"] \arrow[d] & D_i \arrow[d, "p"] & Y\times\mathbb A^1 \arrow[l, hook', "u"'] \arrow[d] \\
\{\infty\} \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb P^1 & \mathbb A^1 \arrow[l, hook']
\end{tikzcd}
```

For the full blowup family, write $E=\mathbb P(C_XY\oplus1)$ and
$W=\mathbb P(C_XY)$. Its infinity fibre is the divisor $B+E$, with each
summand occurring once. The second diagram shows the closed inclusions into
that fibre and their common boundary $W=B\cap E$. Removing $B$ leaves
$E\setminus W=C_XY$, the special fibre of $D_i$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large]
W \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, hook] & E \arrow[d, hook] \\
B \arrow[r, hook] & M_\infty
\end{tikzcd}
```

The projective completion $E$ is a projectivized cone in general; no regular
immersion is assumed in either diagram. Only under the regular-immersion
hypothesis stated above is $C_XY=N_{X/Y}$ a vector bundle. At the level of
cycles, flat pullback along $Y\times\mathbb A^1\to Y$ raises dimension from
$m$ to $m+1$; localization lifts this class to $A_{m+1}(D_i)$ and $j^!$
lowers dimension to $m$, yielding the stated $\sigma_i$. The chart and
localization arguments above establish these facts independently of the
figures.

steps.before: 2.1 For (3) let $B\to C$ be an $A$-algebra map. ## Remarks

The ring maps underlying base change and localization fit into the following commutative squares. Write $f\colon A\to B$ for the given map and $g\colon A\to A'$ for the base-change map.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"g"'] & B \arrow[d,"i"] & A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"\ell_A"'] & B \arrow[d,"\ell_B"] \\
A' \arrow[r,"j"'] & B' & V^{-1}A \arrow[r,"\bar f"'] & U^{-1}B
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $i(b)=b\otimes1$ and $j(a')=1\otimes a'$. The left square is the tensor-product pushout of [F2]: $i(f(a))=j(g(a))$. On the right, $\ell_A(a)=a/1$, $\ell_B(b)=b/1$, and $\bar f(a/v)=f(a)/f(v)$; the hypothesis $f(V)\subseteq U$ makes $\bar f$ well defined. This square commutes because both paths take $a$ to $f(a)/1$.

For $B'=B\otimes_AA'$, the differential comparison is the commutative triangle of $B'$-modules below. The tensor product in its upper-left corner is over $B$, whereas the two differential modules on the right have different base rings.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
B'\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A} \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[dr,"\varphi"',"\cong"] & \Omega_{B'/A} \arrow[d,"q"] \\
& \Omega_{B'/A'}
\end{tikzcd}
```

The map $\alpha$ is the functorial comparison of (3) for $i$, and $q$ sends $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A}x$ to $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}x$. Thus $q\alpha=\varphi$: on $1\otimes\mathrm{d}b$, both paths give $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}(b\otimes1)$, as in step 2.1. Only $\varphi$ is marked as an isomorphism here. Its inverse is induced by the $A'$-derivation $D(b\otimes a')=a'(1\otimes\mathrm{d}b)$ from step 1.1. For localization, step 1.2 instead uses $D(b/u)=u^{-1}\mathrm{d}b-bu^{-2}\mathrm{d}u$ and identifies $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}$ with $\Omega_{U^{-1}B/V^{-1}A}$; [F3] identifies its source with $(U^{-1}B)\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}$.

## Remarks

For the chase in step 4.1, fix $n$ and abbreviate $J=\mathfrak m^n$, $A=(I\cap J)\otimes_R M$, $B=(I\otimes_R M)\oplus(J\otimes_R M)$ and $C=(I+J)\otimes_R M$. For an ideal $L$, write $\mu_L:L\otimes_R M\to M$ for multiplication. The following diagram displays the right-exact tensor row and its compatibility with multiplication:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
A \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I\cap J}"'] & B \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,"\mu_I\oplus\mu_J"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I+J}"] & 0 \\
M \arrow[r,"\delta"'] & M\oplus M \arrow[r,"\sigma"'] & M \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $\alpha(x)=(i(x),-j(x))$, where $i:A\to I\otimes_R M$ and $j:A\to J\otimes_R M$ are induced by the ideal inclusions; $\beta$ is induced by addition into $I+J$. The lower maps are $\delta(m)=(m,-m)$ and $\sigma(u,v)=u+v$. Both squares commute: multiplication agrees with each ideal inclusion, and multiplication after addition equals the sum of the two multiplication maps. The top row is exact by [F20]; no injectivity of $\alpha$ is asserted.

For $k\in K$ as in step 4.1, $\mu_{I+J}\beta(k,0)=\mu_I(k)=0$. The injectivity of $\mu_{I+J}$ from step 3.1 gives $\beta(k,0)=0$, so exactness lifts $(k,0)$ to some $x\in A$. Thus $i(x)=k$ and $j(x)=0$, and $\mu_{I\cap J}(x)=\mu_Jj(x)=0$. The diagram illustrates this lift and its sign convention; the rigorous proof above is independent of the figure.

## Remarks

Put $W=U\cap V$ and suppress the common coefficient ring $R$. With the orientations on $U$, $V$ and $W$ restricted from $M$, the commuting ladder is

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large, /tikz/font=\Large, labels={font=\large}]
H_c^p(W) \arrow[r, "{(e_U,-e_V)}"] \arrow[d, "D_W"'] & H_c^p(U)\oplus H_c^p(V) \arrow[r, "e_U+e_V"] \arrow[d, "D_U\oplus D_V"] & H_c^p(M) \arrow[r, "\delta"] \arrow[d, "D_M"] & H_c^{p+1}(W) \arrow[d, "D_W"] \\
H_{n-p}(W) \arrow[r, "{(i_{U*},-i_{V*})}"'] & H_{n-p}(U)\oplus H_{n-p}(V) \arrow[r, "i_{U*}+i_{V*}"'] & H_{n-p}(M) \arrow[r, "{(-1)^{p+1}\partial}"'] & H_{n-p-1}(W)
\end{tikzcd}
```

steps.before: 4.1 Base change and finite flat normalization. Consider a cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$ proper and $g:Y'\to Y$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$, and write $f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$. For an integral $d$-dimensional $V\subseteq X$, put $W=\overline{f(V)}$ and $e=\dim V-\dim W$. If $e>0$, both $g^*f_*[V]$ and $f'_*g'^*[V]$ are zero: every component of the flat pullback of $V$ has dimension $d+n$, while its image has dimension at most $\dim W+n<d+n$. If $e=0$, set $m=[k(V):k(W)]$. For each component $W_i$ of $g^{-1}(W)$, let $C_i$ be the Artinian local ring of $W\times_Y Y'$ at its generic point. Flat pullback gives coefficient $\ell(C_i)$ on $[W_i]$. The generic algebra of $V\times_Y Y'$ over $C_i$ is $C_i\otimes_{k(W)}k(V)$, a free $C_i$-module of rank $m$. Decomposing it into its Artinian local factors shows that the sum of the generic lengths of the components above $W_i$, weighted by their function-field degrees over $k(W_i)$, is $m\ell(C_i)$. These are precisely the coefficients of $[W_i]$ in $f'_*g'^*[V]$ and $g^*f_*[V]$, respectively. Hence the base-change identity holds on cycles and therefore on Chow groups. Finally, if $f$ is finite flat of constant degree $n$ between integral schemes of the same dimension, then $f$ is dominant and $[k(X):k(Y)]=n$, so $f_*[X]=n[Y]$ by step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The base-change assertion in step 4.1 involves two squares. The first is
Cartesian, with $X'=X\times_Y Y'$ and the two projections $g'$ and $f'$:

```tikzcd
[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large]
X'=X\times_Y Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'"']
& X \arrow[d, "\textstyle f"] \\
Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g"'] & Y
```

Here $f\circ g'=g\circ f'$. The vertical maps are proper, and the horizontal
maps are flat of pure relative dimension $n$. Pushforward follows the vertical
arrows, whereas flat pullback reverses the horizontal arrows. Thus the second
square has the following directions and dimension indices:

```tikzcd
[column sep=huge, row sep=large, font=\Large]
Z_d(X) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'^*"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f_*"']
& Z_{d+n}(X') \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'_*"] \\
Z_d(Y) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g^*"'] & Z_{d+n}(Y')
```

Its commutativity is $f'_*g'^*=g^*f_*$, proved in step 4.1; the same square
holds with $A$ in place of $Z$. The degree is dimension, so proper pushforward
preserves the index and flat pullback increases it by $n$. This does not
assert that proper pushforward preserves codimension. For an integral
$V\subseteq X$, the equal-dimensional case retains the full coefficient
$m=[k(V):k(W)]$, where $W=\overline{f(V)}$: the generic-length computation in
step 4.1 gives $m\ell(C_i)$ at each component $W_i$ above $W$. No assumption
that these field degrees or generic lengths equal one is made, including
over a nonclosed field. In the dimension-drop case both routes give zero.
The diagrams illustrate the maps and their grading; the proof above remains
independent of them.

steps.before: 8.1 Sections of smooth morphisms. Let $s:T\to P$ be a section of a smooth morphism $P\to T$ of constant relative dimension $r$, with $T$ locally Noetherian. Near a point $t\in T$, [F8] factors $P\to T$ Zariski locally as an étale morphism $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_T[x_1,\dots,x_r]$ followed by the projection, after shrinking around $s(t)$ and $t$; by [F7] the étale morphism is flat. The composite $T\to P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ is the graph of the $T$-point with coordinates $c_i=s^*(x_i)$. This graph is cut out by the regular sequence $x_1-c_1,\dots,x_r-c_r$: after quotienting by the first $i$ terms, the next element is a monic linear polynomial in a new variable and hence a nonzerodivisor over any base ring. Pulling the graph back along the flat étale map $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ gives a regular immersion $Q=T\times_{\mathbb A^r_T}P'\hookrightarrow P'$ of codimension $r$, and $Q\to T$ is étale. The section factors through a section $T\to Q$ of this étale morphism. By [F8], after shrinking near the chosen point, this section is described by a standard étale chart $\operatorname{Spec}((A[z]/(P))_g)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $z\mapsto a$, $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)$ a unit. Factoring $P(z)=(z-a)Q_0(z)$ gives $Q_0(a)=P'(a)$; after restricting to the open neighborhood where $Q_0$ is invertible, the equation $P(z)=0$ forces $z=a$, so the section is an open immersion there. Hence near its image in $P'$, the pulled-back regular equations cut out $s(T)$, proving that $s$ is a regular immersion of codimension $r$. These equations remain regular after every base change $T'\to T$, since the section of the smooth base change $P\times_TT'\to T'$ is again locally obtained by this graph construction, including when $T'$ is singular. The normal bundle also commutes with base change: for a section of a smooth morphism, the conormal bundle identifies with $s^*\Omega^1_{P/T}$, and this relative differential bundle pulls back to $s'^*\Omega^1_{(P\times_TT')/T'}$. Hence the codimension and normal bundle are preserved by arbitrary base change on $T$. [F7, F8, algebra] ∎

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The two exact sequences in step 4.1 are sequences of locally free
$\mathcal O_X$-modules. Write $\alpha([f])=1\otimes df$ and let $\beta$ be
restriction of differentials to $X$. Their ranks are respectively $d,m,n$, with $d=m-n$:

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
0 \arrow[r] & \mathcal I/\mathcal I^2 \arrow[r, "\alpha"] & i^*\Omega^1_{Y/k} \arrow[r, "\beta"] & \Omega^1_{X/k} \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

Applying $\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(-,\mathcal O_X)$ reverses the order;
$T_X=(\Omega^1_{X/k})^\vee$ and
$N_{X/Y}=(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)^\vee$. There is no identification of a
bundle with its own dual in these pictures. The dual ranks are $n,m,d$:

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
0 \arrow[r] & T_X \arrow[r, "\beta^\vee"] & i^*T_Y \arrow[r, "\alpha^\vee"] & N_{X/Y} \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

For the coordinate model of step 5.1, put $X_U=X\cap U$ and use coordinates
$(z_1,\ldots,z_d,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ on $\mathbb A^m_k$.
The étale map $\varphi$ pulls $z_j$ back to $f_j$ and $v_a$ back to $u_a$.
The following square is Cartesian: its bottom inclusion is cut out by
$z_1=\cdots=z_d=0$.

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
X_U \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi|_{X_U}"'] & U \arrow[d, "\varphi", "\mathrm{etale}"'] \\
\mathbb A^n_k \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb A^m_k
\end{tikzcd}
```

To see how this model controls the deformation blowup, restrict to the
chart $\mathbb A^1_t\subset\mathbb P^1_k$ on which $t=0$ is $\infty$.
Set $V=U\times_k\mathbb A^1_t$, $M=\mathbb A^m_k\times_k\mathbb A^1_t$,
$C=X_U\times_k\{0\}$ and $C_0=\mathbb A^n_k\times_k\{0\}$.
Thus $C_0\subset M$ has ideal $(z_1,\ldots,z_d,t)$, whose inverse image
under $\psi=\varphi\times\operatorname{id}$ is the ideal
$(f_1,\ldots,f_d,t)$ of $C$. Write $B_V=\operatorname{Bl}_C V$ and
$B_M=\operatorname{Bl}_{C_0}M$. Step 6.1 and flat base change give the
Cartesian square

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
B_V \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\pi_V"'] & B_M \arrow[d, "\pi_M"] \\
V \arrow[r, "\psi", "\mathrm{etale}\ (\mathrm{hence\ flat})"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The vertical arrows are the blowup morphisms; the top arrow is the base
change of $\psi$, so is étale. This identifies $B_V$ with
$V\times_M B_M$, rather than identifying the global blowup with the model.
The $d+1$ model charts are the $t$-chart with coordinates
$(z_1/t,\ldots,z_d/t,t,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ and, for each $1\le j\le d$, the
$z_j$-chart with coordinates
$(z_j,(z_l/z_j)_{l\ne j},t/z_j,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$; each has $m+1$ coordinates.
All affine spaces and products in these pictures are over the given field
$k$; no assumption that $x$ is $k$-rational is made. The bundle ranks are
those over $\mathcal O_X$, or dimensions after tensoring with $\kappa(x)$,
not the local-ring dimensions $m-\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(x)$ and
$n-\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(x)$ of step 1.1. These diagrams illustrate
steps 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1; the proof above remains independent of them.

steps.before: 1.2 Conversely, assume every filtered colimit functor is exact. Let $I$ be a small directed poset indexing a family of monomorphisms $b_i:B_i\rightarrowtail A$, and let $c:C\rightarrowtail A$ represent a fixed subobject of $A$. For each $i\in I$, form the pullback square ```tikzcd P_i \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\ B_i \arrow[r, "b_i"'] & A. ``` By [L4], the top-left leg represents $B_i\wedge C$. These pullback squares assemble into a diagram in $\mathcal A^I$. Because the filtered colimit functor $\operatorname*{colim}_I$ is exact, [L2] and [L3] say that it preserves finite limits, so its colimit square ```tikzcd P \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\ B \arrow[r, "b"'] & A ``` is again a pullback. [L2, L3, L4, assume-hyp, construct]
steps.after: 1.2 Conversely, assume every filtered colimit functor is exact. Let $I$ be a small directed poset indexing an increasing family of monomorphisms $b_i:B_i\rightarrowtail A$, and let $c:C\rightarrowtail A$ represent a fixed subobject of $A$. For each $i\in I$, form $P_i=B_i\times_A C$ with projections $p_i:P_i\to B_i$ and $q_i:P_i\to C$, so $b_i p_i=cq_i$; the composite represents $B_i\wedge C$ by [L4]. For $i\le j$, the inclusion $u_{ij}:B_i\to B_j$ induces the unique $v_{ij}:P_i\to P_j$ with $p_jv_{ij}=u_{ij}p_i$ and $q_jv_{ij}=q_i$. Thus the pullback squares form a diagram indexed by $I$. Set $B=\operatorname*{colim}_I B_i$ and $P=\operatorname*{colim}_I P_i$, with induced maps $p:P\to B$, $q:P\to C$, and $b:B\to A$. The colimits of the constant diagrams at $A$ and $C$ are canonically $A$ and $C$, since $I$ is nonempty and directed. Exactness and [L2] therefore imply that the induced square, with relation $bp=cq$, is again a pullback, namely $P\cong B\times_A C$. The same preservation of finite limits makes $b$ monic, since the natural transformation $(b_i):(B_i)\to\operatorname{const}_I A$ is pointwise monic. Both squares are illustrated in Remarks. [L2, L3, L4, assume-hyp, construct]

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The first square is the pullback defining $P_i$ in step 1.2; the second is its filtered-colimit square. The labels are the maps defined there, and both squares commute: $b_i p_i=cq_i$ and $bp=cq$. In the second square, $B=\operatorname*{colim}_I B_i$ and $P=\operatorname*{colim}_I P_i$, while $A$ and $C$ arise from constant diagrams. The pullback property of the second square uses the assumed exactness of $\operatorname*{colim}_I$.

```tikzcd
P_i \arrow[r, "q_i"] \arrow[d, "p_i"'] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\
B_i \arrow[r, "b_i"'] & A
```

```tikzcd
P \arrow[r, "q"] \arrow[d, "p"'] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\
B \arrow[r, "b"'] & A
```

## Remarks

The supplied orientation makes both nonzero rows constant-coefficient rows.
On page $n+1$, the following schematic shows two columns of these rows;
all intermediate rows are zero. Here $a\geq0$ and the diagonal arrow has
bidegree $(n+1,-n)$.

```tikzcd
[font=\Large, labels={font=\large}, row sep=3em, column sep=4em]
E_{n+1}^{a,n}=H^a(B;R)u \arrow[dr, "d_{n+1}" description] & E_{n+1}^{a+n+1,n}=H^{a+n+1}(B;R)u \\
E_{n+1}^{a,0}=H^a(B;R) & E_{n+1}^{a+n+1,0}=H^{a+n+1}(B;R)
```

For $x\in H^a(B;R)$ the diagonal sends $xu$ to
$(-1)^a x\smile e(p)$; at $a=0$ it sends $u$ to $e(p)$.
Taking its cokernels in the bottom row and kernels in the top row gives the
two stable terms of proof step 3.1. Their short exact filtration sequence
then gives (1): $p^*$ factors through the bottom-row cokernel, while $p_!$
is the top-row quotient followed by its inclusion, using the orientation,
into $H^{k-n}(B;R)$. The cup maps in (1) retain its stated sign normalization.
The schematic neither asserts a splitting of the filtration nor identifies
$p_!$ with a cohomological axis edge; the proof above is independent of it.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

For a fixed coefficient group $G$, the following exact-row fragment displays
all three types of naturality square, including the degree-lowering connector.
Here $i_*$ is induced by subspace inclusion, $q_*$ by the quotient of chain
complexes, $f_A=f|_A:A\to B$, and $f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$ is the relative homology
map induced by $[c]\mapsto[f_\#c]$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[font=\Large, labels={font=\large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
H_n(A;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"] \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"'] &
H_n(X;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"] \arrow[d, "f_*"] &
H_n(X,A;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{X,A}"] \arrow[d, "f_{\mathrm{rel},*}"] &
H_{n-1}(A;G) \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"] \\
H_n(B;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"'] &
H_n(Y;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"'] &
H_n(Y,B;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{Y,B}"'] &
H_{n-1}(B;G)
\end{tikzcd}
```

The right square says $(f_A)_*\delta_{X,A}=\delta_{Y,B}f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$.
For a relative cycle represented by $c$, the connector is represented by
$\partial c$ in the subspace, and $f_\#\partial c=\partial f_\#c$ gives this
identity with no extra sign. These are relative chain quotients, not a claim
identifying relative homology with the homology of a quotient space. The proof
above is independent of the diagram.

## Remarks

The Cartesian square underlying step 1.1 is displayed with $f_i$ on the
right and $f_j$ below, as in that step. Its projections are
$p(x_i,x_j)=x_i$ and $q(x_i,x_j)=x_j$.

```tikzcd
[font=\LARGE, every label/.append style={font=\Large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
Z_{ij}=X_i\times_E X_j \arrow[r, "p"] \arrow[d, "q"'] & X_i \arrow[d, "f_i"] \\
X_j \arrow[r, "f_j"'] & E
```

The defining condition $f_i(x_i)=f_j(x_j)$ gives
$f_i\circ p=f_j\circ q$. Here $p$ is the base change of $f_j$, while $q$
is the base change of $f_i$; both projections are proper. In this orientation,
the extraordinary proper base-change comparison of [F1] is
$f_i^!f_{j!}\cong p_*q^!$, with both sides taking complexes on $X_j$ to
complexes on $X_i$. This square illustrates the adjunction chain; the proof
and its degree calculation remain independent of the figure.

terminal_source_heading.before_suffix:
$\square$ ## Source qualification

Stacks Project Lemma 33.12.3 (tag 038V), lines 23–38, gives the affine-chart characterization of geometric regularity and its finite purely inseparable field tests. Lemma 33.12.6 (tag 038X), lines 23–28, proves that geometric regularity at a point is equivalent to smoothness there for a locally finite-type scheme. The latter statement does not assume perfectness; perfectness enters this item through the regular-algebra scalar-extension theorem. Stacks Algebra Lemma 10.166.1 (tag 0381), lines 22–36, gives the finitely-generated-field versus finite-purely-inseparable test. The stronger arbitrary-field scalar-extension assertion used here is supplied by the fully proved library item [[thm-ag-geometric-regularity-perfect-base]] via [[lem-ag-geometric-regularity-field-tests]].

Milne, *Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter 10 supplement, §f, item 10.64 (printed p. 18 / PDF page 18), states that a regular variety over a perfect field is smooth and that a smooth variety is regular. Milne's “variety” conventions are narrower than the present claim about arbitrary finite-type schemes and do not include this proof's nonreduced dual-number boundary; that citation is corroboration for the classical case, not a substitute for the scheme-level chart argument above.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The pullback used in step 1.1 is the following commutative square, with $P=B\times_C K$ and $p\pi'=k_h\pi$:

```tikzcd
P \arrow[r, "\pi'"] \arrow[d, "\pi"'] & B \arrow[d, "p"] \\
K \arrow[r, "k_h"] & C\vphantom{g_j}
```

The pushout used in step 1.2 is the following commutative square, with $R=Q\amalg_{A'}B'$ and $\iota q_f=\iota'i'$:

```tikzcd
A' \arrow[r, "i'"] \arrow[d, "q_f"'] & B' \arrow[d, "\iota'"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "\iota"] & R\vphantom{g_j}
```

The proof constructs $\delta$ through $\delta\pi=q_fa$, where $a:P\to A'$ satisfies $i'a=g\pi'$. Both squares illustrate the constructions; the proof establishes the connecting relation and uniqueness independently of the figures.

```tikzcd

0 \arrow[r] & A_{n+1} \arrow[r, "f_{n+1}"] \arrow[d, "\alpha_{n+1}"'] & B_{n+1} \arrow[r, "g_{n+1}"] \arrow[d, "\beta_{n+1}"'] & C_{n+1} \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\gamma_{n+1}"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A_n \arrow[r, "f_n"'] & B_n \arrow[r, "g_n"'] & C_n \arrow[r] & 0
```

## Remarks

The triangle displays reassociation through the common set of triples. Write $L=(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP$, $T=M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$, and $\alpha=\alpha_{M,N,P}$. The set maps are $q_L(m,n,p)=(m\otimes n)\otimes p$ and $q_T(m,n,p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p)$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\large]
M\times N\times P \arrow[d, "q_L"'] \arrow[dr, "q_T"] & \\
(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP \arrow[r, shift left=1, "\alpha"] & M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP) \arrow[l, shift left=1, "\beta"]
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $\beta(m\otimes(n\otimes p))=(m\otimes n)\otimes p$. Thus $\alpha q_L=q_T$, $\beta q_T=q_L$, $\beta\alpha=\mathrm{id}_L$, and $\alpha\beta=\mathrm{id}_T$. Both $q_L$ and $q_T$ identify $(mr,n,p)$ with $(m,rn,p)$ for $r\in R$, and $(m,ns,p)$ with $(m,n,sp)$ for $s\in S$, by the balancing relations and the commuting actions on $N$. The diagram illustrates the maps constructed in the proof; the proof is independent of the figure.

## Remarks

The five-term diagram used in step 1.1 makes the five-lemma application visible. Write $D^k(X)=H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)$, $S^k(X)=H_\infty^k(X;\mathbb R)$, $D^k(U,V)=D^k(U)\oplus D^k(V)$ and $S^k(U,V)=S^k(U)\oplus S^k(V)$. Here $W=U\cap V$, and $I_{U,V}=I_U\oplus I_V$ in the indicated degree.

```tikzcd
D^{q-1}(U,V) \arrow[r,"s_D"] \arrow[d,"I_{U,V}"'] & D^{q-1}(W) \arrow[r,"\Delta_D"] \arrow[d,"I_W"] & D^q(M) \arrow[r,"r_D"] \arrow[d,"I_M"] & D^q(U,V) \arrow[r,"s_D"] \arrow[d,"I_{U,V}"] & D^q(W) \arrow[d,"I_W"] \\
```

## Remarks

The first two degrees and the augmentations form the following commutative ladder. Here $j_n$ and $q_n$ are the inclusion of the first summand and projection onto the second summand, and $d_n$ denotes the middle differential. The two projective rows are split exact; the bottom row is the original short exact sequence and need not split. The columns continue upwards to the full resolutions.

```tikzcd
0 \arrow[r] & P'_1 \arrow[r, "j_1"] \arrow[d, "d'_1"'] & P'_1\oplus P''_1 \arrow[r, "q_1"] \arrow[d, "d_1"] & P''_1 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "d''_1"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & P'_0 \arrow[r, "j_0"] \arrow[d, "\varepsilon'"'] & P'_0\oplus P''_0 \arrow[r, "q_0"] \arrow[d, "\lambda_0"] & P''_0 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\varepsilon''"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A' \arrow[r, "i"] & A \arrow[r, "p"] & A'' \arrow[r] & 0
```

The augmentation is $\lambda_0=[i\varepsilon',s]$, where $s:P''_0\to A$ is a chosen lift with $ps=\varepsilon''$. Thus $\lambda_0j_0=i\varepsilon'$ and $p\lambda_0=\varepsilon''q_0$. In positive degrees the chain-map identities are $d_nj_n=j_{n-1}d'_n$ and $q_{n-1}d_n=d''_nq_n$; the chosen summand splittings need not be chain maps. In particular, the middle differential need not be block diagonal.

Writing $K_0=\ker\lambda_0$, $K'_0=\ker\varepsilon'$ and $K''_0=\ker\varepsilon''$, and $K_n=\ker d_n$ with the analogous primed notation for $n\geq1$, each stage gives $0\to K'_n\to K_n\to K''_n\to0$. The next epimorphism $P'_{n+1}\oplus P''_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow K_n$, followed by $K_n\hookrightarrow P'_n\oplus P''_n$, is $d_{n+1}$. Hence consecutive vertical maps compose to zero, including $\lambda_0d_1=0$. This illustrates steps 1.1 and 2.1; the proof is independent of the diagram.

That filtration is zero at $p=-1$ and all of $H_n(T)$ at $p=n$ for $n\ge0$. For $n=0$ there is only one possible quotient, and for the zero complex all pages and quotients are zero. The argument uses no infinite exactness or AC. [F1, F5, step 3.1] ∎

remarks.after:
## Remarks

In this low-degree part of the first-quadrant grid, the original horizontal
index increases to the right and the original vertical index increases upward.
Every square anticommutes: $hv=-vh$; the squares are not asserted to commute.

```tikzcd
C_{0,2} \arrow[d,"v"'] & C_{1,2} \arrow[l,"h"'] \arrow[d,"v"'] & C_{2,2} \arrow[l,"h"'] \arrow[d,"v"] \\
C_{0,1} \arrow[d,"v"'] & C_{1,1} \arrow[l,"h"'] \arrow[d,"v"'] & C_{2,1} \arrow[l,"h"'] \arrow[d,"v"] \\
C_{0,0} & C_{1,0} \arrow[l,"h"'] & C_{2,0} \arrow[l,"h"']
```

The grid continues upward and to the right; components with a negative index
are zero. The cutoff $F^{\mathrm{row}}_1T$ retains rows $0$ and $1$, and its
quotient by $F^{\mathrm{row}}_0T$ retains only row $1$. More generally the
row-$p$ quotient has $E^0_{p,q}=C_{q,p}$ and differential $h$. Taking horizontal
homology turns the downward arrows into the following part of the page-one chain, for
any fixed $q\ge0$:

```tikzcd
E^1_{2,q}=H^h_q(C_{*,2}) \arrow[d,"d^1=v_*"] \\
E^1_{1,q}=H^h_q(C_{*,1}) \arrow[d,"d^1=v_*"] \\
E^1_{0,q}=H^h_q(C_{*,0})
```

Here $v_*[x]=[vx]$, with no additional sign because the total differential
is $h+v$. Thus $d^1$ has bidegree $(-1,0)$ in spectral coordinates, and the
chain continues upward, and its homology at index $p$ is $E^2_{p,q}=H^v_p(H^h_q(C))$.
These diagrams illustrate the filtration and page calculation; the proof above
is independent of them.

## Remarks

Write the two short exact sequences as $0\to A_\bullet\xrightarrow{i}B_\bullet\xrightarrow{p}C_\bullet\to0$ and $0\to A'_\bullet\xrightarrow{i'}B'_\bullet\xrightarrow{p'}C'_\bullet\to0$, with vertical chain maps $a:A_\bullet\to A'_\bullet$, $b:B_\bullet\to B'_\bullet$, and $c:C_\bullet\to C'_\bullet$. For every integer $n$, the associated long exact ladder contains the following commutative portion; the rows continue in both directions.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large, every label/.append style={font=\normalsize}]
H_n(A) \arrow[r, "H_n(i)"] \arrow[d, "H_n(a)"'] & H_n(B) \arrow[r, "H_n(p)"] \arrow[d, "H_n(b)"] & H_n(C) \arrow[r, "\partial_n"] \arrow[d, "H_n(c)"] & H_{n-1}(A) \arrow[d, "H_{n-1}(a)"] \\
H_n(A') \arrow[r, "H_n(i')"'] & H_n(B') \arrow[r, "H_n(p')"'] & H_n(C') \arrow[r, "\partial'_n"'] & H_{n-1}(A')
\end{tikzcd}
```

The first two squares express the chain-map compatibilities $bi=i'a$ and $cp=p'b$ after passing to homology. The third is the connecting-map identity $H_{n-1}(a)\partial_n=\partial'_n H_n(c)$ from [L2], with the same connecting-map convention as the long exact sequence. The proof above is independent of this illustration.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

For the simultaneous outer actions, write ${}_SM_R$ and ${}_RN_T$, and put $Q=M\otimes_RN$. Fix $s\in S$ and $t\in T$. The maps $L_s:Q\to Q$ and $R_t:Q\to Q$ are additive endomorphisms given by $L_s(m\otimes n)=(sm)\otimes n$ and $R_t(m\otimes n)=m\otimes(nt)$. The following square illustrates descent, where $\tau(m,n)=m\otimes n$ and $u_{s,t}(m,n)=(sm,nt)$. The upper row is a map of sets; $\tau$ is a balanced pairing, rather than an additive homomorphism from the product group.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
M\times N \arrow[r, "u_{s,t}"] \arrow[d, "\tau"'] & M\times N \arrow[d, "\tau"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "L_s\circ R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Indeed, $(s(mr))\otimes(nt)=((sm)r)\otimes(nt)=(sm)\otimes r(nt)=(sm)\otimes((rn)t)$. Together with additivity in each variable, this shows that the upper-then-right pairing respects the $R$-balance relation, so it induces the lower map on the tensor quotient. Setting $t=1_T$ or $s=1_S$ recovers the individual action maps. Both orders of applying the outer actions give $(sm)\otimes(nt)$, as in proof step 4.1:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"] \arrow[d, "L_s"'] & Q \arrow[d, "L_s"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Every arrow in this second square is a homomorphism of underlying abelian groups. Its commutativity is $L_s\circ R_t=R_t\circ L_s$ on all of $Q$, since elementary tensors generate $Q$. These illustrations do not replace any part of the proof.

## Remarks

For the simultaneous outer actions, write ${}_SM_R$ and ${}_RN_T$, and put $Q=M\otimes_RN$. Fix $s\in S$ and $t\in T$. The maps $L_s:Q\to Q$ and $R_t:Q\to Q$ are additive endomorphisms given by $L_s(m\otimes n)=(sm)\otimes n$ and $R_t(m\otimes n)=m\otimes(nt)$. The following square illustrates descent, where $\tau(m,n)=m\otimes n$ and $u_{s,t}(m,n)=(sm,nt)$. The upper row is a map of sets; $\tau$ is a balanced pairing, rather than an additive homomorphism from the product group.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
M\times N \arrow[r, "u_{s,t}"] \arrow[d, "\tau"'] & M\times N \arrow[d, "\tau"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "L_s\circ R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Indeed, $(s(mr))\otimes(nt)=((sm)r)\otimes(nt)=(sm)\otimes r(nt)=(sm)\otimes((rn)t)$. Together with additivity in each variable, this shows that the upper-then-right pairing respects the $R$-balance relation, so it induces the lower map on the tensor quotient. Setting $t=1_T$ or $s=1_S$ recovers the individual action maps. Both orders of applying the outer actions give $(sm)\otimes(nt)$, as in proof step 4.1:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"] \arrow[d, "L_s"'] & Q \arrow[d, "L_s"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Every arrow in this second square is a homomorphism of underlying abelian groups. Its commutativity is $L_s\circ R_t=R_t\circ L_s$ on all of $Q$, since elementary tensors generate $Q$. These illustrations do not replace any part of the proof.

$$\langle\mathcal Fu_f,\varphi\rangle =\int f(x)\!\left(\int\varphi(\xi)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi\right)dx =\int\widehat f(\xi)\varphi(\xi)\,d\xi.$$

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The diagram displays how the chart maps fit together. For distinct indices
$i,j$, write $X_{ij}=X_{s_i}\cap X_{s_j}$ and $U_{ij}=U_i\cap U_j$.
The horizontal arrows are open inclusions; the vertical arrows are the
constructed morphisms, with $\varphi_{ij}$ their common restriction to the
overlap. The open sets $X_{s_i}$ cover $X$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={nodes={font=\Large}}, every label/.append style={font=\large}]
X_{ij} \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi_{ij}"'] & X_{s_i} \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi_i"] & X \arrow[d, "\varphi"] \\
U_{ij} \arrow[r, hook] & U_i \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb P^n_S
\end{tikzcd}
```

Both squares commute by steps 2.1 and 3.1. The same diagram with $i,j$
interchanged describes the other chart. On $X_{ij}$ the change of coordinates
is exactly
$$x^{(j)}_\ell\circ\varphi_j=\frac{s_\ell/s_i}{s_j/s_i}=\frac{s_\ell}{s_j}\quad(\ell\ne i,j),\qquad x^{(j)}_i\circ\varphi_j=\frac{1}{s_j/s_i}=\frac{s_i}{s_j}.$$
The denominator is invertible on this overlap. Likewise the frame relation
$e_j=x^{(i)}_je_i$ pulls back to $s_j=(s_j/s_i)s_i$, so the local
identifications $\varphi^*\mathcal O(1)\cong L$ agree, as checked in step 4.1.
The diagram asserts no immersion property for a vertical arrow. The proof
above is independent of the illustration.

Nothing in the construction asserts injectivity or immersion: two distinct points may have proportional tuples, and $\varphi$ is an immersion only under additional hypotheses. If some $s_i=0$ then $X_{s_i}=\varnothing$ and the corresponding local piece is empty, which the gluing of step 3.1 allows; if all $s_i=0$ the hypothesis that they generate $L$ fails unless $X=\varnothing$, and then the construction is vacuous. The Axiom of Choice [A1] is inherited from the projective-space and associated-sheaf constructions; no choice is made here. [A1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, cases: vanishing sections and empty X] ∎

## Remarks

The diagram displays how the chart maps fit together. For distinct indices
$i,j$, write $X_{ij}=X_{s_i}\cap X_{s_j}$ and $U_{ij}=U_i\cap U_j$.
The horizontal arrows are open inclusions; the vertical arrows are the
constructed morphisms, with $\varphi_{ij}$ their common restriction to the
overlap. The open sets $X_{s_i}$ cover $X$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={nodes={font=\Large}}, every label/.append style={font=\large}]
X_{ij} \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi_{ij}"'] & X_{s_i} \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi_i"] & X \arrow[d, "\varphi"] \\
U_{ij} \arrow[r, hook] & U_i \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb P^n_S
\end{tikzcd}
```

Both squares commute by steps 2.1 and 3.1. The same diagram with $i,j$
interchanged describes the other chart. On $X_{ij}$ the change of coordinates
is exactly
$$x^{(j)}_\ell\circ\varphi_j=\frac{s_\ell/s_i}{s_j/s_i}=\frac{s_\ell}{s_j}\quad(\ell\ne i,j),\qquad x^{(j)}_i\circ\varphi_j=\frac{1}{s_j/s_i}=\frac{s_i}{s_j}.$$
The denominator is invertible on this overlap. Likewise the frame relation
$e_j=x^{(i)}_je_i$ pulls back to $s_j=(s_j/s_i)s_i$, so the local
identifications $\varphi^*\mathcal O(1)\cong L$ agree, as checked in step 4.1.
The diagram asserts no immersion property for a vertical arrow. The proof
above is independent of the illustration.

The top row below uses $\mathcal C$-coordinates and the bottom row uses $\mathcal B$-coordinates; each matrix acts by left multiplication on a coordinate column.

```tikzcd
M_{n\times1}(F) \arrow[r, "B"] \arrow[d, "P"'] & M_{n\times1}(F) \arrow[d, "P"] \\

```

The square commutes because both paths describe applying $T$ and expressing the result in $\mathcal B$-coordinates: $AP=PB$, equivalently $B=P^{-1}AP$. The proof above is independent of this illustration.

## Remarks

The butterfly comparison is induced by the two inclusions of the common meet. With $M=A_1\wedge B_1$, $U=A_1\wedge B_0$, $V=A_0\wedge B_1$, and $S=U\vee V$, it is pictured by the following commuting squares.

```tikzcd
A_0\vee M \arrow[d, "q_L"'] & M \arrow[l, hook', "i_L"'] \arrow[r, hook, "i_R"] \arrow[d, "p"] & M\vee B_0 \arrow[d, "q_R"] \\
\frac{A_0\vee M}{A_0\vee U} & M/S \arrow[l, "\alpha"', "\sim"] \arrow[r, "\beta", "\sim"'] & \frac{M\vee B_0}{V\vee B_0}
```

Here $i_L$ and $i_R$ are the canonical inclusions, and $q_L$, $p$, and $q_R$ are the quotient maps by $A_0\vee U$, $S$, and $V\vee B_0$, respectively. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 identify the kernels of $q_L i_L$ and $q_R i_R$ with $S$. Both composites are epimorphisms, so they induce the isomorphisms $\alpha$ and $\beta$ characterized by $\alpha p=q_L i_L$ and $\beta p=q_R i_R$. The displayed isomorphism in the statement is $\beta\alpha^{-1}$. The proof above is independent of this illustration.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The following grids show the two augmentations separately. Horizontal arrows
increase the Čech degree $p$; downward arrows increase the resolution degree
$q$. The arrows are the **unsigned** maps, so each displayed square commutes.
The first grid lies in $\tilde D$: its left column has degree $p=-1$, and
$r^q=h^{-1,q}$ denotes restriction of global sections.

```tikzcd
\Gamma(X,G^0) \arrow[r,"r^0"] \arrow[d,"{\Gamma(X,d^0)}"'] & D^{0,0} \arrow[r,"h^{0,0}"] \arrow[d,"v^{0,0}"'] & D^{1,0} \arrow[d,"v^{1,0}"] \\
\Gamma(X,G^1) \arrow[r,"r^1"'] & D^{0,1} \arrow[r,"h^{0,1}"'] & D^{1,1}
```

The second grid lies in $E$ from proof step 1.4: its top row has degree
$q=-1$, and $w^p=C^p(\mathcal U,\varepsilon)$ is induced componentwise by the
Godement coaugmentation.

```tikzcd
C^0(\mathcal U,\mathcal F) \arrow[r,"\delta^0"] \arrow[d,"w^0"'] & C^1(\mathcal U,\mathcal F) \arrow[d,"w^1"] \\
D^{0,0} \arrow[r,"h^{0,0}"'] & D^{1,0}
```

For totalization, the downward arrow in column $p$ is multiplied by $(-1)^p$;
in particular it has sign $-1$ in the extra column $p=-1$. This is the
sign convention in the Statement, rather than a sign on the commuting grids.
The comparison maps assemble as follows:

```tikzcd
\Gamma(X,G^\bullet) \arrow[r,"u"] & \mathrm{Tot}D & C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F) \arrow[l,"w"']
```

Here $u$ enters column $p=0$ through $r^q$, while $w$ enters row $q=0$
through $w^p$. The first comparison is always a quasi-isomorphism under the
Statement's hypotheses; the second is a quasi-isomorphism when the cover is
$\mathcal F$-acyclic. These illustrations record the constructions and
conclusions of the Statement and proof steps 1.4, 6.1 and 7.1; the proof is
independent of the figures.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

For the lifting construction in steps 1.1–2.1, let $I=[0,1]$ and let $\alpha:I\to E$ be a loop at $e_0$ whose image under $p$ is nullhomotopic as a based loop. Choose a homotopy $H:I\times I\to B$ with $H(s,0)=p(\alpha(s))$, $H(s,1)=b_0$, and $H(0,t)=H(1,t)=b_0$. With $i_0(s)=(s,0)$, the lifting problem is:

```tikzcd
I \arrow[r, "\alpha"] \arrow[d, "i_0"'] & E \arrow[d, "p"] \\
I\times I \arrow[r, "H"'] \arrow[ur, dashed, "\widetilde H" description] & B
```

The square commutes because $H\circ i_0=p\circ\alpha$. Its dashed lift satisfies $p\circ\widetilde H=H$ and $\widetilde H\circ i_0=\alpha$ by [F1]. Uniqueness on the two side edges forces $\widetilde H(0,t)=\widetilde H(1,t)=e_0$; uniqueness on the final edge then forces $\widetilde H(s,1)=e_0$. Thus $\widetilde H$ is a homotopy of based loops from $\alpha$ to the constant loop at $e_0$. The diagram illustrates the lifting construction; the proof above remains independent of it.

The naturality identity says that the following square commutes. The vertical maps are the canonical evaluation maps, and the lower map is the transpose of $T^*$.

```tikzcd
X \arrow[r, "T"] \arrow[d, "J_X" swap] & Y \arrow[d, "J_Y"] \\
X^{**} \arrow[r, "T^{**}" swap] & Y^{**}
```

Both paths from $X$ to $Y^{**}$ send $x$ to the functional $g\mapsto g(Tx)$ on $Y^*$, as computed in steps 1.1–2.1.

technique.after: **Proof technique:** For 1 < p < ∞, test the Radon-Nikodym density against bounded truncated extremizers and pass to the limit by monotone convergence. For p = 1, level-set testing forces the essential supremum below the operator norm.

## Remarks

For $n=p+q$, the following exact window displays the initial couple with all index shifts visible:

```tikzcd
D^1_{p-1,q+1} \arrow[r, "i"] & D^1_{p,q} \arrow[r, "j"] & E^1_{p,q} \arrow[r, "k"] & D^1_{p-1,q} \arrow[r, "i"] & D^1_{p,q-1}
```

Here $i$ is induced by $F_{p-1}C\hookrightarrow F_pC$, $j$ by $F_pC\twoheadrightarrow F_pC/F_{p-1}C$, and $k$ is the connecting morphism. Thus the last $D$ term has total homological degree $n-1$, as does the target of $k$. The figure records the sequence and exactness established in steps 2.1–3.1; the proof is independent of it.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The triangle illustrates the free extension of the product-indexed family. Write $u_{(i,j)}$ for the standard vector of $R^{(I\times J)}$, and let $\iota(i,j)=u_{(i,j)}$ and $b(i,j)=e_i\otimes f_j$. The diagonal is a set map; $\Phi$ is the module isomorphism of the statement.

```tikzcd
I\times J \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "b"'] & R^{(I\times J)} \arrow[d, "\Phi", "\cong"'] \\
& M\otimes_R N
```

The triangle commutes because $\Phi(u_{(i,j)})=e_i\otimes f_j$, as traced in proof step 3.1. More generally, for every finitely supported coefficient family $(c_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$,

$$\Phi\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}u_{(i,j)}\right)=\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}(e_i\otimes f_j).$$

These sums are finite even when $I$ and $J$ are infinite. If either index set is empty, the top-left set is empty and both module vertices are zero, as in step 3.2. The given bases suffice; no further choice of basis is involved. The proof above is independent of the illustration.

## Remarks

For a $T$-invariant subspace $W$, the induced operator makes the following square commute. Both vertical arrows are the canonical projection $\pi(v)=v+W$.

```tikzcd
V \arrow[r, "T"] \arrow[d, "\pi"'] & V \arrow[d, "\pi"] \\
V/W \arrow[r, "\bar T"'] & V/W
```

Indeed, $\pi(T(v))=T(v)+W=\bar T(\pi(v))$ for every $v\in V$. The well-definedness and linearity proof in [[prop-induced-quotient-operator-is-well-defined]] is independent of this illustration.

## Remarks

Let $n=\dim V$, and write $\kappa_{\mathcal B}:V\to F^n$ for
$v\mapsto[v]_{\mathcal B}$, with $\kappa_{\mathcal C}$ defined similarly.
Here $F^n$ is identified with the coordinate-column space $M_{n\times1}(F)$.
The coordinate-change identity in step 1.1 is the commutativity of this square;
the bottom arrow denotes multiplication by the displayed matrix.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large, scale=1.8, transform shape]
V \arrow[r, "\mathrm{id}_V"] \arrow[d, "\kappa_{\mathcal B}"'] & V \arrow[d, "\kappa_{\mathcal C}"] \\
F^n \arrow[r, "P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}"'] & F^n
\end{tikzcd}
```

The reverse coordinate conversion is multiplication by
$P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal C}$. Step 3.1 gives both compositions:

$$P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal C}P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}=I_n,\qquad P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal C}=I_n.$$

Thus the two bottom coordinate spaces are inverse identifications of the same
vector space, including when $n=0$. The proof above is independent of the figure.

4.1 Derive Riesz representation with the linear-first convention. If $z\in\ker\varphi$, then $y+t z\in M$ for every scalar $t$, and minimality gives [L1, L2, step 3.1]

$$d^2\leq\|y+t z\|^2=d^2+2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl(t\langle z,y\rangle\bigr)+|t|^2\|z\|^2.$$

If $\langle z,y\rangle\ne0$, choosing the scalar phase of a sufficiently small $t$ to make the middle term negative contradicts this inequality. Therefore $\langle z,y\rangle=0$. For arbitrary $x\in H$, the vector $z=x-\varphi(x)y$ lies in $\ker\varphi$, and linearity in the first argument now gives $\langle x,y\rangle=\varphi(x)\|y\|^2$. Hence

$$\varphi(x)=\langle x,R\varphi\rangle,\qquad R\varphi:=y/\|y\|^2.$$

Together with $R0=0$, this represents every functional. Uniqueness follows by evaluating the difference of two representing vectors at that same difference. Cauchy--Schwarz and the unit vector in the representing direction give $\|R\varphi\|=\|\varphi\|$.

5.1 Put the transported Hilbert structure on the dual. Define $C:H\to H^*$ by $(Cx)(u)=\langle u,x\rangle$. Step 4.1 says that $C$ is onto with inverse $R$, and [L1] shows that both are conjugate-linear in the complex case and linear in the real case. They are isometries. Define on $H^*$ [L1, L4, step 4.1, construct]

$$\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle_*:=\langle R\psi,R\varphi\rangle_H.$$

The reversed order and the two conjugate-linear occurrences make this inner product linear in $\varphi$, conjugate-linear in $\psi$, and positive definite; its norm is the existing dual norm. By [L4], $H^*$ is complete for that norm, so it too is a Hilbert space.

remarks.before:
## Remarks

- **Which route this proof takes, and why.** The extension is obtained by re-running the construction of [[thm-r-uncountable]] with a new seed, not by transporting uncountability along a bijection. The reason is that there is nothing to transport: the theorem states that $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable and nothing more, and no item of this library states that $[0,1]$ is uncountable, so the affine order-isomorphism $t \mapsto a + t(b-a)$ from $[0,1]$ onto $[a,b]$ has no uncountable source to carry across. Re-running is available instead precisely because the theorem's proof is already general: its step 2.1 builds the trisection rule $T$ for an arbitrary $(a,b) \in I$, and its steps 4.1 to 7.1 quote only the nesting $a_n \le a_{\sigma(n)}$, $b_{\sigma(n)} \le b_n$, the strictness $a_n < b_n$ and the omission $f(n) \notin [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$. Its step 1.1, the seed of its step 3.1 and the conclusion of its step 7.1 are the special ones, and they are the three replaced here: a surjection onto $(a,b)$ rather than onto $\mathbb{R}$, the seed $(0,(p,q))$ rather than $(0,(0,1))$, and a conclusion about the interval rather than about $\mathbb{R}$.
- **A corollary of the argument, not of the statement.** That distinction is the whole content of the previous remark, and it is why the proof is written out here in full rather than replaced by a citation. deltas.after:
## Statement

Let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of groups on a topological space $X$, let
$U \subseteq X$ be open, and let $s\in\mathcal F(U)$. Then

$$
s=0\text{ in }\mathcal F(U)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad s_x=0\text{ in }\mathcal F_x\text{ for every }x\in U.
$$

remarks.before:
## Remarks

- Claim 2 is the fact used constantly in practice: an equation between classes may always be replaced by a relation between representatives, and conversely. Claim 3 is what makes a quotient set behave like a set of disjoint boxes.

- The converse half is what licenses building an equivalence relation by describing its classes rather than its pairs. The uniqueness clause matters: it says that no information is lost either way, so a partition and an equivalence relation are interchangeable descriptions of the same structure.

deltas.before:
## Remarks

- Claim 2 is the fact used constantly in practice: an equation between classes may always be replaced by a relation between representatives, and conversely. Claim 3 is what makes a quotient set behave like a set of disjoint boxes.

- The converse half is what licenses building an equivalence relation by describing its classes rather than its pairs. The uniqueness clause matters: it says that no information is lost either way, so a partition and an equivalence relation are interchangeable descriptions of the same structure.
